title: Writing a paragraph in Turkish
subtitle: How to write a paragraph at B1–B2 — an opinion, a comparison, a personal story or advice — what the grader looks for and how to deliver it.

text.text: Every attempt is scored on four criteria, and each one counts. A paragraph with perfect grammar that ignores half the prompt scores low; so does a well-organised answer full of agreement errors. Aim for a balance.
— did you answer the prompt, cover every required element, take a clear position where one is asked for, and stay inside the word range?
— does the paragraph have a clear opening, supporting points and a conclusion, and do connectors show how each idea relates to the last?
— is your word choice precise and varied, and does it fit the register (informal or formal) of the task?
— are verb forms, agreement and word order correct, and do you use some more complex structures (subordinate clauses, a range of tenses) accurately?
80–120 words, 15 minutes on the timer.
150–200 words, 25 minutes on the timer.
Going far over the maximum does not earn extra credit — it usually means padding or repetition, and going over the length band also costs you on Task achievement.
Many B1–B2 prompts are open questions with no right answer. Before you write a word, decide
you will answer — then build the whole text around that decision.
There are two. The wording of the prompt usually signals the better fit; when either works, pick the one you can argue best:
— argue one side and answer the strongest objection to it. Use it when the prompt asks for your view: "give your opinion", "do you agree…?", "should…?".
— weigh both sides fairly, then say where you land. Use it when the prompt asks you to "discuss the advantages and disadvantages" or to "compare".

children.text: Either way, commit from the first sentence.

text.text: A balanced answer is not a way to avoid answering: it still ends with a clear judgement.
Both approaches use the same four moves:
— restate the question in your own words, then give your position (stance) or say what you will weigh up (balanced).
— one main reason, backed by an example or a consequence.
— with a stance, raise the strongest counter-argument and answer it; with a balanced view, give the other side fairly.
— answer the question directly. No new arguments.

children.text: Fitting it to the word range.

text.text: At

(150–200 words), write four short paragraphs: an introduction and a conclusion of about 30–40 words each, and two body paragraphs of about 40–55 words each — the primary point usually runs longest. At

(80–120 words), the same four moves fit in 6–8 sentences, one or two per move. Put them in one paragraph or in four very short ones: short paragraphs make the structure visible, and either is fine within 80–120 words.

The question:
(should cars be banned in city centres?). This answer takes a strong stance. It is 164 words — B2 length (150–200) — in four paragraphs, shown one sentence at a time.

body.en: These days, banning cars in city centres is often debated.

note.text: Restates the question in your own words.

target.text: Bu tartışma, trafik sorunu arttıkça özellikle büyük şehirlerde daha da önem kazanıyor.

body.en: As traffic problems grow, this debate is becoming even more important, especially in big cities.

note.text: Says why the question matters.

target.text: böyle bir yasak hem çevre hem de insan sağlığı için gerekli,

body.en: In my opinion, such a ban is necessary both for the environment and for people's health, but it should be implemented carefully.

note.text: Your position, from the first paragraph.

target.text: , arabasız bir şehir merkezi herkes için daha sağlıklı ve daha keyiflidir.

body.en: First of all, a car-free city centre is healthier and more pleasant for everyone.

note.text: The primary point.

target.text: Hava daha temiz olur, gürültü azalır ve insanlar rahatça yürüyebilir ya da bisiklete binebilir.

body.en: The air becomes cleaner, the noise goes down and people can walk or cycle comfortably.

note.text: The reason behind it.

body.en: Moreover, people lead a more active life because they walk more.

note.text: A further benefit that supports the same point.

target.text: İstanbul'daki İstiklal Caddesi yıllardır trafiğe kapalı ve her gün yüz binlerce insan orada özgürce dolaşıyor.

body.en: For example, İstiklal Avenue in Istanbul has been closed to traffic for years, and every day hundreds of thousands of people stroll there freely.

note.text: A concrete example.

target.text: Yaşlıların, engellilerin ve şehir dışında yaşayanların arabaya gerçekten ihtiyaç
bu sorunun da bir çözümü var.

body.en: It is true that older people, disabled people and those who live outside the city really need a car, but this problem has a solution too.

note.text: Raises the strongest objection and starts to answer it:

target.text: Belediyeler toplu taşımayı geliştirebilir, merkezin dışında otoparklar yapabilir ve bu gruplara özel izinler verebilir.

body.en: Municipalities can improve public transport, build car parks outside the centre and give special permits to these groups.

note.text: Answers the objection with concrete steps.

target.text: kimse mağdur olmadan şehir merkezi yayalara açılabilir.

body.en: In this way, the city centre can be opened to pedestrians without anyone losing out.

target.text: , şehir merkezlerinde arabaların yasaklanması hem bugün için hem de gelecek nesiller için doğru bir karardır.

body.en: In conclusion, banning cars in city centres is the right decision, both for today and for future generations.

note.text: Answers the question directly.

target.text: Şehirler arabalar için değil, insanlar için vardır.

body.en: Cities exist for people, not for cars.

note.text: Sums up the primary point in one line.

target.text: bu değişiklik adım adım ve gerçek alternatiflerle yapılmalı.

body.en: But the change must be made step by step and with real alternatives.

note.text: Restates the condition from the introduction — no new argument.

text.text: A strong opinion paragraph has three parts: an
that states your position,
(each backed by a reason or an example, and ideally one point that admits the other side), and a
that restates your view.
The same three-part shape works for every kind of prompt. What changes is the job of the opening sentence:
— states your position.
— names the two things and the point (or points) you will compare them on.
— sets the scene: when, where and who.
— states the problem and your main recommendation.

The supporting points and the closing sentence follow the same pattern: in a comparison, each point compares the two options on one feature, and the closing says which suits whom; in a story, the points are what happened, in order, and the closing says how it ended or what you learned; in advice, each point is a reason or a concrete step.
Here is a model paragraph answering
(is remote work a good idea?), one sentence at a time. It is 97 words — B1 length. A B2 answer would develop each point further.

target.text: Bence uzaktan çalışmanın avantajları dezavantajlarından daha fazladır.

body.en: In my opinion, remote work has more advantages than disadvantages.

note.text: Opening sentence: states the position clearly.

target.text: , uzaktan çalışan kişiler işe gidip gelmek zorunda olmadıkları

body.en: First of all, people who work remotely save a lot of time because they don't have to commute.

note.text: Supporting point 1, with a reason:
(because they …).

target.text: , İstanbul'da yaşayan bir arkadaşım eskiden her gün trafikte iki saat geçiriyordu; şimdi bu zamanı spora ayırıyor.

body.en: For example, a friend of mine who lives in Istanbul used to spend two hours in traffic every day; now she devotes that time to sport.

note.text: A concrete example backing point 1.

target.text: , birçok kişi evde daha sakin bir ortamda çalıştığı

body.en: Moreover, many people can focus better on their work because they work in a calmer environment at home.

note.text: Supporting point 2.

target.text: var: Uzun süre evde tek başına çalışan insanlar kendilerini yalnız hissedebilir.

body.en: However, remote work also has some risks: people who work alone at home for a long time may feel lonely.

note.text: Supporting point 3 admits the other side.

target.text: şirketlerin çalışanlarını düzenli olarak bir araya getirmesi önemlidir.

body.en: That is why it is important for companies to bring their employees together regularly.

note.text: Draws a consequence from the objection.

target.text: haftanın birkaç günü evden çalışmak bence en iyi çözümdür.

body.en: In conclusion, although remote work has some difficulties, working from home a few days a week is, in my view, the best solution.

note.text: Closing sentence: restates the position in a more precise form, with a concession (

text.text: The connectors (highlighted) carry the argument: they tell the reader which sentence is a new point, which is an example, and where the paragraph turns to the other side. Notice that some of them work in two pieces: a suffix that turns the verb into a noun (
), followed by a separate word (
). See the next section.
Here is a model paragraph for a comparison prompt,

children.text: "Şehirde yaşamak mı daha iyi, köyde yaşamak mı?"

text.text: (is it better to live in a city or in a village?), one sentence at a time. It is 104 words — B1 length (80–120). Each supporting point compares the two options on one feature, and one point names a similarity, not only differences.

target.text: Şehirde yaşamakla köyde yaşamak arasında özellikle iş imkânları, hayat pahalılığı ve sosyal hayat açısından önemli farklar vardır.

body.en: There are important differences between living in a city and living in a village, especially in terms of job opportunities, the cost of living and social life.

note.text: Opening sentence: names the two options and the three points of comparison (
= in terms of).

target.text: Şehirde iş bulmak genellikle daha kolaydır ve maaşlar daha yüksektir;

body.en: Finding a job is usually easier in the city and salaries are higher, whereas in the village job opportunities are quite limited.

note.text: Point of comparison 1 (work).
opens the second half and sets it against the first.

target.text: maaşın büyük bir kısmı kiraya gider.

body.en: However, rents in the city are much higher than in the village, so a large part of your salary goes on rent.

note.text: Point of comparison 2 (cost of living).
= compared with the village: the dative
plus

target.text: hızlı internet vardır; bu sayede köyde yaşayanlar da büyük şirketler için uzaktan çalışabiliyor.

body.en: Today, as in the cities, many villages have fast internet too; thanks to this, people who live in a village can also work remotely for big companies.

note.text: Back to work, this time a similarity, not only a difference (
= as is the case in the cities).

target.text: , köyde sinema ve tiyatro gibi kültürel etkinlikler oldukça azdır;

body.en: Nevertheless, cultural activities such as cinema and theatre are quite rare in the village; for this reason, young people often get bored.

note.text: Point of comparison 3 (social life) turns the balance back towards the city.

target.text: , bence kariyer yapmak isteyenler için şehir, sakin ve ucuz bir hayat arayanlar için ise köy daha uygundur.

body.en: In short, in my view the city is more suitable for those who want to build a career, and the village for those looking for a quiet, inexpensive life.

note.text: Closing sentence: says which option suits whom, instead of declaring one simply "better".

text.text: A B2 answer (150–200 words) would extend each point of comparison with an example — a person you know, a price, a typical day.
At B1–B2 the grader looks for
: not just
and
, but connectors that show contrast, consequence and concession — including the suffix-based ones.

items.en: Public transport is cheap; moreover, it pollutes the environment less.
Although the rent is very high, I prefer living in the city centre.
Life in the city is very fast, whereas in the village people live more calmly.
The buses don't run at night. That's why I usually take a taxi.

text.text: (informal),

target.text: bazı şehirler daha fazla bisiklet yolu yapıyor.

items.en: Some cities, such as Copenhagen, are building more cycle paths.
In conclusion, the solution to this problem is in all our hands.

An informal message to a friend:

target.text: Sevgili Ayşe, nasılsın? Uzun zamandır sana yazamadım.

body.en: Dear Ayşe, how are you? I haven't been able to write to you for a long time.

note.text: Formal opening when you don't know the name.

body.en: I am writing to get information about the summer course.

note.text: A standard first line.

sections.title: the task and the word count

text.text: Most prompts list
— things your text must mention. The grader checks each one. Make every element visibly present: give it its own sentence, and use the element's own key word so it cannot be missed.

body.en: One disadvantage of remote work is loneliness.

note.text: Required element "mention a disadvantage" — the key word
makes it impossible to miss.

text.text: Before you write, list the required elements and give each one a sentence. Add your opening and closing sentence to the plan.
Draft the sentences, then join them with connectors so the reasoning is easy to follow.
before you submit, and compare with the range for your level.
Add a reason or a concrete example to your weakest point, or a sentence that admits the other side.
Cut repetition first — sentences that say the same thing twice — not a required element.
These are the errors the grader flags most often at B1–B2. Each example shows the
sentence; the wrong version is in the note.

body.en: After talking to my friends, I made my decision.

note.text: not: *konuştukten sonra*. Suffix vowels follow the last vowel of the stem:

body.en: I have a friend who lives in Istanbul.

note.text: not: *İstanbul'da yaşadığı arkadaşım*. When the noun is the
of the relative clause (the friend lives), use
. Use
only when the noun is the object or a place (
— the city I live in).

target.text: Geçen yıl okuduğum kitap çok ilginçti.

body.en: The book I read last year was very interesting.

note.text: not: *Geçen yıl okudum kitap*. A relative clause with its own subject uses
(past/present) or
(future) plus a possessive ending for the subject (
…), before the noun:
— "the city I will go to tomorrow".

body.en: I finished the book I bought yesterday.

note.text: not: *Dün aldığım kitap bitirdim*. A definite object takes the accusative
; an indefinite one does not:

body.en: I would like to meet with you about this matter.

note.text: not: *İstiyorum sizinle görüşmek bu konuda*. The main verb comes at the end, even in long sentences.

Every required element is present, each in its own sentence.
The word count is inside the range for your level.
There is an opening sentence and a closing sentence.

ideas — and, for a comparison prompt,
The register is consistent from start to finish — you did not switch between informal and formal.
